video_title: Live at Univ. of Oregon: AI and State Governments with Nik Blosser
transcript: Nick, welcome to Scaling Laws. >> Thanks, Kevin. Good to see you. >> Always a pleasure. So, you and I had a tremendous opportunity to be hosted by the AI Student Association at the wonderful University of Oregon. We had an awesome chat with upwards of 30 students organized by Ellie and Maggie, who are the student organizers there behind that great organization. You and I had a delightful chat. It was insightful. We had all of these students asking great questions. And your podcast host made the incredible mistake of forgetting to press record. And Nick, you are living up to the reputation of what we Oregonians like to say, Oregon nice, by agreeing to do another conversation. So, Nick, I just want the audience to know how generous you are with your time and how grateful I am to you for uh being the first second guest on Scaling Laws in such a short matter. So, you're really breaking records here. >> Thanks, Kevin. It's not a problem. I know technical issues happen, and I just I'm sorry that the room full of students isn't in front of us. >> Well, I I share the same because Maggie and Ellie did a great job, but uh we will certainly be back with the AI Student Association at UO sooner rather than later as part of our our roadshow. But, for now, Nick, I want to start with your job. You are the Chief AI Officer of the state of Oregon. And there have been these announcements at the federal level, at the state level, at even at the city level about AI czars, about uh you know, Chief AI uh officers in some cases. But, I think a lot of folks are left asking, "What does that actually mean?" So, if you could just start with what is your job description? [clears throat] And what's included and what's excluded? >> Yeah, when I started about a year ago, my charge was really twofold. It was set a policy framework, set some governance for the safe, responsible use of AI by its by state agencies. And in addition to that, it's then supporting those agencies with evaluating their good ideas and seeing if we can help implement those. It has also expanded it recently into other duties as assigned because AI has become such a headline issue with concerns about AI safety and um I think also opportunities for economic development, business growth, and innovation. So, it's been pretty broad lately. >> I I really think that every AI job, the first bullet point in the job description should be other duties as assigned because everyone is being asked to wear so many hats and adjust and acclimate. But one thing that stands out about your role in the state is that if we went back through the legislative record, even 3 years ago, we wouldn't find reference to Chief AI Officer. Can you walk through where this even came from and and how at a more abstract level, there's this difficulty of even anticipating the need for positions like your own given state budget cycles and just the way the state typically moves both in Oregon and more generally? >> Yes. So, in late 2023, I think after chat GPT first came out, um Oregon's governor issued an executive order and appointed a task force to evaluate AI and what the state should do. That task force issued a report about a year and a half later in February of 2025 and it basically said one of the first thing it said is you should appoint a someone a point person for AI at the state. Um but that did not those recommendations and there were another 40 recommendations in there, as you said, don't really line up with state budget processes. We have a every 2-year budget process that takes another year ahead of time to uh schedule. So, I'm nowhere I don't have I actually don't have a budget. I don't I don't have I'm not in the statute. Uh but the CIO in his wisdom decided we need this. I'm going to create a couple roles and steal from other places. And so that's that's how I live now. But when I want to go do anything, I have to sort of walk around with my hands out to other departments um and ask for help. >> So, you're you're the equivalent of the Oliver of the state of Oregon. Please, sir, may I have some more? But in this case, to the credit of the governor and to the credit of uh Terrance Woods, the CIO for the state of Oregon, they have moved nimbly. They've recognized the need for someone with your skill set and with your background to help plug these holes. And as we'll get into the importance of having someone who can go to state agencies, which also aren't known for moving fast and breaking things. If anything, uh and as a former employee of the state of Oregon, I could say state agencies are perhaps more known for moving slowly and breaking things. Uh but that's a a different conversation or doing their best to maintain things. But with respect to your unique skill set, I'm guessing when your parents asked you when you were five or your third grade teacher asked you, "Hey Nick, what do you want to be when you grow up?" You didn't say, "Oh, I can't wait to serve as the chief AI officer of a state." So, what is it about your background that and and to be fair for our listeners, uh please understand that Nick and I are friends. But Nick, to be blunt, what qualifies you for this job? >> Yeah, good question. You know, I have degrees in both engineering and in English. And I think much of my career has been trying to understand fairly technical topics and then be able to translate them for policy makers or the general public. And I think that's exactly the situation we find ourselves in with artificial intelligence. Which is it's at its core a pretty sophisticated um technology that not not even the practitioners fully understand how it works or why it works. And I think what's what my background has given me is the ability to at least describe what we know, what we don't know, and frame risk in a way that policy makers can understand. How's that for an answer? >> I I I love it. I love it. And I think that I talked to a lot of students right now who are asking, "Professor Frazier, what should I major in or what should I focus on here in law school? Uh show me the path to becoming the next Chief AI Officer of some state." And you are such a great testament to my advice, which is, "Hey, just go be curious and go study things and go demonstrate that you can learn quickly and get stuff done." And I I'd venture to say that the uh path you took of aeronautical engineering and English at Stanford, which you know, doesn't immediately point in this direction. The fact that you have policy experience in energy at the federal and state level. And then also your time serving as the chief of staff to Governor Kate Brown. It's the amalgamation of all of those skills that allow you to navigate this highly ambiguous space. And that to me is going to be the portfolio of skills that really distinguish the folks who get stuff done in AI rather than the folks who are, you know, "Oh, I took all 15,000 hours of whatever YouTube videos I could find on the subject." And that's the thing that I'm going to try to do to to move into this field. And I wonder if you could explain just a little bit further how you think your time being in the White House, serving as the chief of staff for a governor. What is it about that policy background that you found has translated well into this domain? >> Yeah, good questions. I think, you know, and some of the students came up after our our last recording and asked me sort of what their advice was, too. And I my I encouraged them to actually spend some time in the private sector. A lot of people who work in government, particularly on the Democratic side, don't tend don't have private sector experience. And I think that's invaluable. Just to understand how businesses think, how corporate boards work. >> [clears throat] >> What it What is What is the CEO and the board of a publicly traded company? What kind of pressures are they under? And you see this every day now with several of the frontier labs, including ones that are about to go public. Um at the governor's office, there's no substitute to sort of watching policy and how it gets made at that level. And just knowing, I mean, the state of Oregon is like any state, an amalgamation or a confederation of about 100 different businesses, business units. It's got prisons and parks. It's got state police, health authority. It's got such a diversity, and that's even more so at the federal level. So, I think just having an appreciation for the diversity of types of employees, um types of policy questions that governments face, and also the real impact that those decisions can have on people and businesses. I think that is probably the most the the the experience that has helped me most and help and developing AI policy that that works for that diversity and isn't one size fits all because it can't be. >> Yeah, and I really like your point about the need to make sure that you are hyper aware of what the technology is actually being used for and who's going to deploy it, which is something that often gets lost in the sauce. Uh we had a conversation with a very astute individual who came up to us after our recording in Eugene and said, "Hey, you know, I'm a little concerned that the state of Oregon is thinking how to deploy AI and how do we know that this isn't going to result in a hugging face 2.0 at the hands of someone like Nick Blosser?" Uh and there's this conflation of anytime folks hear the words AI, they think, "Oh my gosh, it must be frontier tools that are being deployed for the most sensitive use cases." But you and I were kind of riffing on this idea and I'd love for you to walk through it in more detail of the importance of making AI boring. Right? There's there's this temptation to associate anything that's new and novel with lots of risk, lots of uncertainty. And yes, there are aspects of AI that may always be somewhat unknowable or somewhat of a black box. But what does it look like from a agency standpoint to think through deploying a really boring AI system and how do you try to translate that to the leadership there and their employees? >> Yeah, good question. So, we have a process where an agency has an idea of of a piece of software that they want to buy or build or use and they fill out an IT investment form that asks a bunch of questions and now they fill out an AI use form. And it asks a bunch of questions. Um and those questions are aimed at triaging the risk. So, one of the questions is is your AI system going to be internal facing or external facing? Is the public going to interact with it? If if it's public facing, we consider that higher risk. Is your AI system going to use publicly available data or confidential data? Personal information. If it's the latter, we would consider that higher risk also. And then it asks questions about where the data resides, where is the data being processed? We require that to be in the United States. And then finally, it'll ask, does it do any of these 20 things that we call rights or safety impacting? Is it involved in decision-making related to someone's employment or someone's benefits? Or is it doing analysis on bridge loadings, which could have a life safety impact? If it's also any of those, we would consider that higher risk. So, almost all of the implementations so far have not been higher risk at the state of Oregon. We have a couple now that we've approved, and I'm happy to talk a little bit more about those. But that's how we help agencies understand how risky their idea might be. >> I and I think that level of specific I think that level of specificity and granularity is so important. And there are some folks who may be listening who are thinking, "Oh my gosh, what a burdensome process. You want to go into the weeds of each and every use case for every agency, for every deployment." And admittedly, at times I've I've thought that myself, right? You hear about startups that spin up and deploy agents to go do X number of tasks with minimal human oversight. But one of the things that's stuck with me throughout this AI wave is the fact that if we want to see mass adoption of these tools and if we want to see AI achieve its promised benefits in healthcare, in medicine, in law, and for things like the improvement of government services, you've got to bring the public along, right? We've seen this and we won't get too into the weeds on data centers, but where you skip steps in a process or even where you are perceived to have skipped steps in a process, you lose trust. And if you lose trust, then you're it's so hard to restore it and it's so hard to bring people back on board. And so for all those folks who are thinking, "Gosh, the state of Oregon, what Luddites." I think instead it's this is what's necessary for Oregonians and for Americans generally to see how and when AI is being used so that they don't immediately think of hugging face and swarms and phase one big being in charge of their Medicaid determinations. So, if you could translate that to the work you all recently did on Medicaid eligibility questions and walk through why you think that's a a good case study for other states perhaps and even the federal government to be aware of. >> Yeah, I say all this this story is going to be under the mantra of we aspire to boring competency. Um and I think a good example, you had some some innovative developers at our health and human services agency. We have about and they had an idea for a new system. We have about a thousand employees who help Oregonians with their eligibility for Medicaid and SNAP. There's about I'm going to make this up, but a thousand pages of policy they have to be familiar with to answer questions and evaluate eligibility, which they do when someone either comes in the office or calls the contact center. This about development team built an internal chatbot that would be able to answer questions that employ these thousand employees had about policy related to Medicaid and snap. So when someone called um and asked a technical question, the human agent would just key it in and get a response with a citation and repeat it back to the caller and that has helped speed up those kind of response times. I think what what has been interesting is it maybe started they did a whole lot of testing before they released it. They first tested with one person, then 10 people, then 50 people before releasing it. And then once it was released to the thousand agents, it was maybe could answer 70% of the questions. But then over time they had built in um a process of updating the the knowledge sources and within three months it was at answering 95% of the questions. So the next extension of that was comfort at the senior level of the agency to do a similar system but for the public. And you know, we would call this higher risk because there's no human intermediary between the AI answering a question that a human might ask. So we have an initial launch of this about a couple weeks ago. It answers questions about Medicaid work requirements that are coming in January. And it was tested exhaustively. It's been monitored now that it's it's live with constant revision. And um you know, I'm just really excited. The last thing maybe I'll add about this is I'm excited that the agency also published a pretty detailed AI system transparency disclosure. And that's one of the things our policy required is to just be really clear in plain language when you have a public-facing AI tool, what what is it? Who owns it? What does it do? What data does it have access to? Um what are the actually stating what you think the risks are and how those were mitigated. And then finally, if you enter something in the chatbot as a as a consumer or user, where does that data store? So, they did a really nice job of that. Um if people want to Google it, it's AI system disclosure for Oregon Medicaid and it's it's a pretty phenomenal document. >> The cool part about that story is I have been so impressed on this road show. Uh we were in North Dakota, we were in Nebraska, we were in New York, uh we were just in Oregon. And hearing about the folks at state governments around the country and at startups and businesses around the country who are being entrepreneurial and innovative. And they're trying to work as quickly and as thoughtfully as they can within institutional safeguards. But it's spots like North Dakota that are saying, "Hey, we're going to make all of our laws and bills and legislative hearing materials machine-readable." And it's states like Oregon that are coming up with disclosure forms that make it easier for innovative employees to be able to say, "Hey, I have an idea for a potential AI use case." And if you have these processes in place, well, then the next great idea can occur much more smoothly. And so, one of the things that I have been riffing on and I would appreciate your take on this is there's certainly real concerns about the capacity of the good folks in uh Salem, Oregon, the good folks in Helena, Montana, the good folks in Sacramento, you name the capital, identifying the people who want to come do innovative work in a state government. It's not always the ideal location, it's not always the ideal pay. How have you found identifying the right talent and recruiting and retaining that talent to begin to push the frontier of of how government can be improved uh in in some of the ways you're already recognizing? >> Yeah, it's a good question. We I have a very small team and I just hired someone who's fantastic. She came from the federal government. So, there's actually a lot of opportunity in hiring federal employees right now at the state level. Um I think having having a even a role on a small team like mine that's willing to help these entrepreneurs that are in these agencies not get stuck by bureaucracy is probably the main thing that I'm I really try to do to help them to not just identify them, but then help them. Some of that comes down to making sure they have the right tools uh to be able to do what they want to do and sometimes having the right tools means that our office has reviewed and approved them for security purposes as an example. >> And when you think about what it means to get the information you need both from a procurement standpoint and from a upskilling your own staff standpoint, one of the things you mentioned earlier was there are certain questions for which we just don't know what we don't know. And that's a scary place for any smart person to be. And one of the frustrations that you and I discussed and that I've ranted about uh ad nauseam on this podcast is the need for vastly more information sharing between the labs and folks like yourself. You know, there's uh efforts that are being made and should be applauded to do things like external engagement, to post YouTube videos, uh to have blog posts, and all of that is great. But what does it look like from the vantage point of a chief AI officer? When you say, "Hey Anthropic, hey OpenAI, hey Microsoft, we really need your help understanding this tool. Can you walk through how responsive are they? Are they sending the right people? If you could use this platform to, you know, scroll a message to them, what would it be? What would you like to see labs doing more of for our folks like yourself uh and in similar roles? >> Yeah, good question. So, our governor, similar to other states, several states have passed laws asking for greater disclosure, third-party or independent review of frontier intelligence. Several states like ours issued executive orders to that effect. So, I was charged about a month ago with delivering a report in 90 days summarizing recommendations of how the state of Oregon could only purchase frontier intelligence, artificial intelligence that had been third-party or independently reviewed. So, I've been on a mission the last couple months, last month, talking with the frontier labs, with value independent evaluators, with academics, trying to understand the latest on that topic and how people are approaching it. And what has become clear is that there's just significant information asymmetry. The handful of labs have incredible R&D that they're doing. They built incredible products. But the government, the public sector that's in charge of safeguarding people and the planet really doesn't have visibility into the latest and greatest of what they're doing. All we see are young AI engineers resigning, saying that there's a 10% chance humanity's going to not make it. And um so that raise, you know, our radar goes up and we're like, "Okay, let's go learn and find out." And so, for a thoughtful group of folks, which I like to think of myself as not trying to be too reactionary, that's a really hard position to be in because we're kind of begging these these labs to tell us, "What are you doing there? How do you define third-party and independent?" And I'll say, like I've I've had initially good response to talking and have definitely reached the limit of what they're willing to do voluntarily. And I think that's where I'll I'll sort of end with a quick anecdote, which is we're talking to one of the labs and they have agreements with They've announced agreements with third parties to come in and do evaluation. And part of that evaluation and is that the evaluator will will be able to release their report to the public, but there was an asterisk, uh you know, with certain restrictions. And so, I asked the lab, "Well, what are those restrictions?" And there was some hand-waving and they're like, "Well, you know, it has to do with security and IP." And I said, "Well, could we see the copy of the contract you have with that evaluator so we can understand exactly what restrictions you put on them." And basically, after a pause, it was The answer was no. Now, I'm going to go back and maybe we'll get it, but I don't know how we can call anything independent or third-party reviewed if we don't even know that that this independent evaluator is restricted or free to say what's on their mind. >> And this is a chief frustration of mine, which is the labs talk a lot about using AI to transform society. And here you are the chief AI officer who's helping a state with parks, prisons, higher education, K-12, you name it, saying, "Hey, I have folks here in Oregon who are ready to deploy AI, but they need to know certain aspects about these tools, and they need to be able to understand them, and first and foremost, I, Nick Blosser, need to be able to to understand this and kick the tires. And yet, please correct me if you think I'm I'm off base here, but it seems to me like so much of the industry and even so many of the independent verification organizations are so hyper-focused on frontier risks, which are very concerning. If if indeed there's even a 1% chance of the end of humanity in 20 years, we would want significant resources being spent there. But we also have to find some way, if this talent is so concentrated in what I like to call the Silicon Tower, if everyone's in San Francisco and if they're only focused on the frontier, and they're not saying, "What is the boring information that Nick Blosser needs to know in Oregon and Justice Tuffy needs to know in North Dakota?" Then you all are just waiting for those nibblets, the the mana from heaven of whatever the information is required, and that to me seems to be a a huge concern that we've yet to see addressed in terms of building out an AI ecosystem for the purpose of, as you and I discussed, making government boring again. Right? We need verifiers who can say things like, "Yes, this is good for Medicaid eligibility. I'm not investigating the extent to which it's going to cause hugging face 2.0." Right? Those are are different skill sets and a different sort of dynamic that needs to be established. >> Yeah, let me say let me let me say a couple things about that. One, I I do feel for the staffers at these labs because they are under a lot of pressure. A bunch of them are going to do IPOs, a bunch of them, you know, they're all publicly traded or soon will be, and they have a lot of pressures there to to act a certain way, which is why it's so important that the public sector have both access and expertise to be able to call balls and strikes on the risk. Because literally you've got certain people saying there's no risk at all and other people saying 10% of the of the world is going to die and that is an impossible place to put put government that doesn't have access or expertise right now. I do think it's useful to break apart the what I think about the AI sort of assurance or landscape. I think of it in kind of a couple different two main buckets. One is frontier intelligence, like you said. And there you have the lab itself, the model testing before it gets released, and then the model after it's released to monitor it. But the second category is what I'll just call an AI system. That AI system is using it could be a a new model, it could be an older model, but it's using a system to take actions and potentially make decisions. And that's where states that's where I thought I would be spending more of my time is evaluating risk and security around AI systems. And there's both digital systems and in the future there'll be robotics and physical systems like, you know, autonomous driving is an AI system. And so one of the things that we had been spending and will still be spending time on is third-party evaluation of AI systems that are in the higher risk categories that I delineated. And that's when I think of these independent evaluators, they're the ones that I think are beginning to There's beginning to be enough of them that they can come in and evaluate an AI system for for example, compliance with federal non-discrimination law. You don't have to call it woke AI, you can just call it compliance with federal non-discrimination law and most states can agree to that. We we need that as well. >> And when you think through getting that sort of broader ecosystem of talent and getting folks to be more comfortable with AI as a result of having more verification, having more granular verification specific to the sorts of deployments you're contemplating, one of the things that sticks with me is this conversation we still have to have around public trust. Which is you may build it, will they come? There was polling that was released by DHM Research for Oregon that looked at what the public generally thinks about some of these AI issues. And some of it was fairly predictable. We saw that there is pretty widespread opposition to data centers. Uh there's unease about AI being used in certain highly sensitive contexts. But then a really interesting finding was when you shifted the framing of how and when AI was going to be used in government services, just the framing of is this going to be something that's replacing or trying to make government efficient in uh sort of language that to me evoked doge-like vibes, Oregonians were opposed to that. But in framing that suggested, hey, let's improve and make government services uh more beneficial and more effective, well, in that those instances, you saw a lot more public support. And so, what are you hearing from Oregonians themselves? Are you all getting tons of letters from Oregonians saying, you know, get rid of this Chief AI Officer? Why do we even have this sort of position? What's your argument to Oregonians about why this office needs to exist? And not to say that you're sending a message to any legislators or, you know, folks with a a pen on the budget out there. But what's the case for even expanding and improving investment in positions like your own? >> Yeah, good question. You know, I primarily have engaged with I would call a microcosm of Oregonians, which is state employees. There's 50,000 state employees. They're diverse group, diverse agencies like we just talked about. And they have a very diverse set of opinions about the appropriate use of AI, fears, and also excitement. And, you know, some of them want are mad that we don't let them do whatever they want with AI. Some of them think we shouldn't do anything with AI, which is kind of mirrors the the the research. So, I think it's again sort of a little bit of boring competency to explain we're not letting you do anything you want. Here's Here's how to think about what you should do, and frankly, you should crawl before you walk or run. And so, I think the only way we gain trust is to build these tools that are extremely well tested and well monitored after they're they're deployed, so that employees get growing confidence in these tools and are then willing to take the next step of maybe like in the case of uh the Medicaid chatbot, using something that was internal facing and making it external facing. So, we're a long way from having AI make any decisions. I don't trust that. No one should trust that right now. But, in terms of helping humans make decisions, I think we're we need to be really thoughtful about that, but I think also reward people with ambitions and good ideas, um and figure out how to help them do it responsibly. If my office didn't exist, if there wasn't a comprehensive policy, I think you would have a free-for-all, and that would be that could be dangerous, and you would have issues. >> And it's worth pointing out that the work you all are doing is so resource and time intensive in a way that I think a lot of states and a lot of external observers may fail to fully recognize, which is to say if you want to build a good AI tool, even for something like Medicaid eligibility, you need so much data to do the testing you described. You need thoughtful people thinking about what are the proper evaluations to assess how is this tool going to do in an edge case? Uh you and I discussed for example, there may be a situation in which an Oregonian is on the verge of some sort of mental collapse because of concerns about whether or not they're going to be uh able to receive certain benefits. How is the tool going to respond in those scenarios? >> Yeah. >> And this is where I want states to be more thoughtful about the full stack of investments that have to be made for AI to go well. It's not only personnel. It's things like making all of the data they already have machine readable. It's finding ways to make sure that data can be shared across diverse actors. And even perhaps in some cases allowing third parties to share more data with the state so that there can be a more comprehensive understanding of which communities are impacted when and how. And so it really is a sort of it takes a village to make good AI. >> Yeah. >> It's certainly true, but that's not something that all lawmakers necessarily understand. That if you have bad AI, it's often because you don't have good data. And good data just doesn't appear out of anywhere. Uh and so I wonder for you as uh Oregon's inaugural chief AI officer, where do you learn best practices from? Uh you mentioned that that you hang out occasionally with a friend of the pod, uh a mutual friend here, Cass Madison. What is Cass up to and how are you engaging with other folks in similar positions to learn how to do your job? >> Yeah, good question. >> Not that you don't know how to do it, how to do your job better. I apologize, Nick. >> In a such a fast I mean, it's impossible to keep up. Honestly, [clears throat] I I listen to scaling laws and a few other podcasts, but it's impossible to keep up, right? Um and Cass and the Center for The Center for Civic Futures is the group she's started and runs now and it is a venue for chief AI officers at states to share good ideas. We meet at least monthly. We have a couple conferences a year. They have a grant program for rewarding grants to states with innovative ideas. So, that's been really helpful. There's a There's a couple other kind of gatherings. The National Association of State CIOs also has a gathering of state um chief AI officers. So, I do, but I think also just talking to my colleagues, I will say back on the data question, I like [clears throat] to think that 80% of the ability for AI to be successful is good data. And the other 80% of secure AI is identity. And those those have historically been boring topics that legislators haven't really understood why and even agency leaders, why are those so important? But if you don't have good data and you don't know who is interacting with that through identity, you're not going to be successful. Um I would say the last thing way I keep up to date is I just on the weekends play with the latest and greatest myself. And you I think there's no substitute and people say this for just diving in and playing around and seeing what these tools can do. And also frankly seeing what they can't do. I think it's important to to get frustrated also to realize these these things are not going to take my job. They're not able to do that, but they are able to with the right instructions, the right data, able to do amazing things. >> Well, consider this an open invitation for any lawmakers who are listening in Oregon or otherwise. If you need an AI demo, I know a guy in Austin who's got a set of wonderful students who would love to do these sorts of AI demos. But more seriously, it is amazing when I go around the country and I talk to judges or lawmakers and I just start with a demo of deep research on open AI or with Anthropic. >> Yeah. >> And showing the incredible capabilities to just learn something new in a rapid fashion and not necessarily say that it's all verified and it's all correct necessarily, but now you're getting a sense of what other questions to be asking, you're broadening your horizons and I think there's just so much work that the future is going to make fun of us for not doing sooner. So for example, running all of our laws through AI to just ask, "What are potential loopholes here? What are potential typos?" Uh I think that's going to be table stakes in in future legislative sessions. Also things like simulations of how might this law go poorly? You know, how might it not uphold in an emergency context or who knows? >> Yeah. >> There are so many cool use cases and that's why I'm so inspired by folks like yourself who are experimenting and being curious and and trying new things. And so for states who are interested in this work, what I would say too is make sure you're a part of Cass's group. Make sure you're talking to folks like Nick, but look to unexpected places. It's so cool. Massachusetts has a data hub. West Virginia is working extensively on better data collection because often times models aren't as performative in uh Appalachia. There's not as much high-quality data there. So, there's a need to be met. And these are all such exciting governance problems and opportunities, but I know I could keep nerding out about that for a while. Nick, I want to close because you can take the boy out of Oregon, but you can't take Oregon out of the boy. And I still care deeply about my home state. And I I I would love to hear your argument for how Oregon can be a real leader in this domain, not only at the state level, but more generally, because yeah, right now you and I have talked about the concentration of power and talent in places like California. And I am wildly concerned that we're not seeing enough other bubbles be created. Uh bubbles in the positive sense here.
